hints: Model each synonym pair as an undirected edge. A word can be replaced by any word in the same connected component, not only by a directly paired word.
Use union-find to merge synonym pairs and collect the words belonging to each component.
For every word in the sentence, build its list of valid replacements, then use backtracking to take one choice from each list and form every sentence.
title: Synonymous Sentences Problem

notes: Each synonym pair is undirected: either word can replace the other.
Transitive synonym relationships are valid through any connected chain of pairs.
The returned sentences must be sorted lexicographically.
constraints: All words consist of at most 10 English letters only.
text consists of at most 10 words.
All pairs of synonyms are unique.
The words of text are separated by single spaces.
content.inputFormat: Single line: JSON array of all arguments, e.g. [arg1, arg2, ...]

sampleTestCases.input: [[["happy","joy"],["sad","sorrow"],["joy","cheerful"]],"I am happy today but was sad yesterday"]
sampleTestCases.output: ["I am cheerful today but was sad yesterday","I am cheerful today but was sorrow yesterday","I am happy today but was sad yesterday","I am happy today but was sorrow yesterday","I am joy today but was sad yesterday","I am joy today but was sorrow yesterday"]
sampleTestCases.explanation: The words happy, joy, and cheerful form one synonym group, while sad and sorrow form another. The 3 × 2 combinations produce 6 sentences.

sampleTestCases.input: [[["happy","joy"],["cheerful","glad"]],"I am happy today but was sad yesterday"]
sampleTestCases.output: ["I am happy today but was sad yesterday","I am joy today but was sad yesterday"]
sampleTestCases.explanation: Only happy and joy are reachable from a word in the sentence, so the sentence has exactly two valid variants.

content.problemStatement:
You are given a list of equivalent string pairs `synonyms` where `synonyms[i] = [s_i, t_i]` indicates that `s_i` and `t_i` are equivalent strings. You are also given a sentence `text`.

Return all possible synonymous sentences sorted lexicographically.

notes: The returned value is a list of strings and must be serialized as a JSON array.
The test constraints keep the number of synonym words small; solutions must still handle transitive components and repeated sentence words correctly.
Synonym equivalence is symmetric and transitive, so connected components capture all valid replacements.
Words that do not occur in any synonym pair remain unchanged.
Sorting each synonym group and the final result guarantees the required lexicographic output order.
solution.approach: Treat synonym pairs as edges of an undirected graph. Because synonym relationships are transitive, every connected component is a synonym group. Build these components with union-find, collect and sort the words in each group, then backtrack through the words of text, choosing every valid synonym for each position. Finally sort the generated sentences lexicographically.

better.complexity: O(W·(W + P) + R·S) time and O(W² + P + R·S) space in the worst case.
better.description: Cache the full reachable synonym set for each distinct synonym word using DFS or BFS once. Reuse those cached sets while backtracking through the sentence. This avoids repeating the same graph traversal for repeated words.

optimal.complexity: O(P α(W) + W log W + R·S + R log R·S) time and O(W + T + R·S) space.
optimal.description: Use union-find to merge each synonym pair in near-constant amortized time. Build the connected components, sort the words in each component, backtrack through the sentence using the corresponding component as the choices for each synonym word, and sort the final sentences.

bruteForce.complexity: O(T·(W + P) + R·S), where T is the number of words in text, P is the number of pairs, W is the number of distinct synonym words, R is the number of generated sentences, and S is the sentence length.
bruteForce.description: Build the synonym graph and, for each occurrence in the sentence, run a graph traversal to find every word reachable from that occurrence. Then recursively enumerate all combinations. This repeats graph exploration whenever the same synonym word appears multiple times.

solution.timeComplexity: O(P α(W) + W log W + R·S + R log R·S), where P is the number of synonym pairs, W is the number of distinct synonym words, R is the number of returned sentences, and S is the sentence length.
solution.spaceComplexity: O(W + T + R·S), where T is the number of words in text; the R·S term is the returned output.

followUps: How can the sentences be generated directly in lexicographic order so that the final result does not need a separate sort?
How would the solution change if the number of synonym pairs and sentence words were much larger?
How could the data structure support synonym-pair updates between multiple queries?
